title: 04. AsyncIO: AsyncIO Basics
summary: Covers Coroutines and await, Creating and Managing Tasks, asyncio.gather() and asyncio.wait(), asyncio.sleep() and Timing, Running Async Code.

diagrams.title: One turn of the event loop
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  ready[("Ready queue")] --> run["Run each ready task until its next await"]
  run --> reg["Awaited I/O is registered with the selector"]
  reg --> poll["selector.select(timeout) — epoll / kqueue / IOCP"]
  poll --> cb["Ready sockets and expired timers schedule callbacks"]
  cb --> ready
diagrams.explain: asyncio runs everything on **one thread**. Each turn, the loop runs every ready task until it hits an `await` on something not yet available, then asks the OS which sockets or timers are ready and schedules the tasks waiting on them. Nothing runs in parallel, so a task that never awaits — a CPU loop or a blocking call — freezes every other task.

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Basic Coroutine

```python
import asyncio

async def greet(name):
    """Simple coroutine that greets a name"""
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Simulate async operation
    print(f"Goodbye, {name}!")
    return f"Greeted {name}"

async def main():
    """Main coroutine"""
    # Await a coroutine - executes it
    result = await greet("Alice")
    print(f"Result: {result}")

# Run the main coroutine
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
Hello, Alice!
Goodbye, Alice!
Result: Greeted Alice
```

#### Example 2: Sequential vs Concurrent Awaits

```python
import asyncio
import time

async def fetch_data(name, delay):
    """Simulate fetching data with delay"""
    print(f"[{name}] Starting fetch...")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(f"[{name}] Done!")
    return f"{name}_data"

async def sequential():
    """Sequential execution - one after another"""
    print("\n=== SEQUENTIAL ===")
    start = time.time()

    # Each await waits for the previous to complete
    result1 = await fetch_data("A", 1)
    result2 = await fetch_data("B", 1)
    result3 = await fetch_data("C", 1)

    print(f"Results: {result1}, {result2}, {result3}")
    print(f"Time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

async def concurrent():
    """Concurrent execution - all at once"""
    print("\n=== CONCURRENT ===")
    start = time.time()

    # Create tasks - they start running immediately
    task1 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("A", 1))
    task2 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("B", 1))
    task3 = asyncio.create_task(fetch_data("C", 1))

    # Wait for all tasks
    result1 = await task1
    result2 = await task2
    result3 = await task3

    print(f"Results: {result1}, {result2}, {result3}")
    print(f"Time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")

async def main():
    await sequential()
    await concurrent()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

Output:

```
=== SEQUENTIAL ===
[A] Starting fetch...
[A] Done!
[B] Starting fetch...
[B] Done!
[C] Starting fetch...
[C] Done!
Results: A_data, B_data, C_data
Time: 3.00s

=== CONCURRENT ===
[A] Starting fetch...
[B] Starting fetch...
[C] Starting fetch...
[A] Done!
[B] Done!
[C] Done!
Results: A_data, B_data, C_data
Time: 1.00s
```

#### Example 3: What You Cannot Await

```python
import asyncio

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# You CAN await:
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def coroutine_example():
    return "from coroutine"

async def main():
    # 1. Coroutines
    result = await coroutine_example()
    print(f"Coroutine result: {result}")

    # 2. Tasks
    task = asyncio.create_task(coroutine_example())
    result = await task
    print(f"Task result: {result}")

    # 3. Futures
    future = asyncio.Future()
    asyncio.get_event_loop().call_soon(lambda: future.set_result("from future"))
    result = await future
    print(f"Future result: {result}")

    # 4. asyncio.sleep()
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    print("Slept!")

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# You CANNOT await:
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

def regular_function():
    return "not awaitable"

async def show_errors():
    # This would raise TypeError!
    # result = await regular_function()  # ❌ TypeError!
    # result = await 42                   # ❌ TypeError!
    # result = await "string"             # ❌ TypeError!

    # Instead, call regular functions normally:
    result = regular_function()  # ✅
    print(f"Regular function result: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
    asyncio.run(show_errors())
```

diagrams.title: From async def to a finished coroutine
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  def["async def fetch()"] -->|"call fetch()"| obj["coroutine object — nothing has run yet"]
  obj -->|"await it or create_task()"| run["running until the next await"]
  run -->|"await on pending I/O"| sus["suspended — loop runs others"]
  sus -->|"I/O ready"| run
  run -->|return| done["finished — value goes to the awaiter"]
  obj -.->|"never awaited"| warn["RuntimeWarning: coroutine was never awaited"]
diagrams.explain: Calling an `async def` function only creates a coroutine object; its body runs when something **awaits** it or wraps it in a Task. Each `await` is a possible suspension point where control returns to the event loop. Forgetting the `await` is the most common asyncio bug — the work silently never happens.

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Creating and Managing Tasks

```python
import asyncio

async def long_task(name, duration):
    """A long-running task"""
    print(f"[{name}] Started")
    try:
        await asyncio.sleep(duration)
        print(f"[{name}] Completed")
        return f"{name}_result"
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print(f"[{name}] Cancelled!")
        raise

async def main():
    # Create tasks
    task1 = asyncio.create_task(long_task("A", 2), name="Task-A")
    task2 = asyncio.create_task(long_task("B", 3), name="Task-B")

    # Check task properties
    print(f"\nTask properties:")
    print(f"task1.get_name(): {task1.get_name()}")
    print(f"task1.done(): {task1.done()}")
    print(f"task1.cancelled(): {task1.cancelled()}")

    # Wait for one task
    result1 = await task1
    print(f"\nTask1 result: {result1}")
    print(f"task1.done(): {task1.done()}")

    # Wait for second task
    result2 = await task2
    print(f"Task2 result: {result2}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: Task Cancellation

```python
import asyncio

async def interruptible_task():
    """Task that can be cancelled"""
    try:
        print("Task started, will run for 10 seconds...")
        for i in range(10):
            print(f"  Working... step {i}")
            await asyncio.sleep(1)
        return "completed"
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("  Task was cancelled!")
        # Cleanup can happen here
        raise  # Re-raise to propagate cancellation

async def main():
    # Create and start task
    task = asyncio.create_task(interruptible_task())

    # Let it run for 3 seconds
    await asyncio.sleep(3)

    # Cancel the task
    print("\nCancelling task...")
    task.cancel()

    # Wait for cancellation to complete
    try:
        await task
    except asyncio.CancelledError:
        print("Task cancellation confirmed")

    print(f"Task cancelled: {task.cancelled()}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 3: Getting All Tasks

```python
import asyncio

async def worker(name, duration):
    """Worker task"""
    await asyncio.sleep(duration)
    return name

async def main():
    # Create several tasks
    tasks = [
        asyncio.create_task(worker(f"Task-{i}", i * 0.5), name=f"Task-{i}")
        for i in range(5)
    ]

    # Get all running tasks
    all_tasks = asyncio.all_tasks()
    print(f"All tasks ({len(all_tasks)}):")
    for t in all_tasks:
        print(f"  - {t.get_name()}: done={t.done()}")

    # Get current task
    current = asyncio.current_task()
    print(f"\nCurrent task: {current.get_name()}")

    # Wait for all
    await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.title: Sequential awaits vs create_task
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant M as main()
  participant L as Event loop
  Note over M,L: Sequential — about 3 seconds
  M->>L: await fetch(a) — 1 s
  M->>L: await fetch(b) — 1 s
  M->>L: await fetch(c) — 1 s
  Note over M,L: Concurrent — about 1 second
  M->>L: create_task(fetch(a)), (b), (c)
  L->>L: all three wait on I/O at the same time
  M->>L: await the tasks or gather them
  L-->>M: three results after about 1 s
diagrams.explain: `await coro` runs one thing at a time. `create_task` schedules the coroutine on the loop **immediately**, so several waits overlap. Keep a reference to every task you create (or use a TaskGroup): the loop only keeps a weak reference, and an unreferenced task can be garbage-collected mid-flight.

sections.title: 8.4 asyncio.gather() and asyncio.wait()
sections.body:
### Visual Explanation

```
╔════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║                    GATHER vs WAIT                                           ║
╠════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║                                                                             ║
║  asyncio.gather():                                                          ║
║  ─────────────────                                                          ║
║  • Runs coroutines/tasks concurrently                                       ║
║  • Returns results IN ORDER                                                 ║
║  • Raises first exception (unless return_exceptions=True)                   ║
║                                                                             ║
║      results = await asyncio.gather(coro1, coro2, coro3)                    ║
║      # results = [result1, result2, result3]  # Ordered!                    ║
║                                                                             ║
║  asyncio.wait():                                                            ║
║  ───────────────                                                            ║
║  • More control over completion                                             ║
║  • Returns (done, pending) sets                                             ║
║  • Can wait for FIRST_COMPLETED, ALL_COMPLETED, FIRST_EXCEPTION            ║
║                                                                             ║
║      done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=...)             ║
║      # done = set of completed tasks                                        ║
║      # pending = set of still-running tasks                                 ║
║                                                                             ║
╚════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝
```

### Code Examples

#### Example 1: asyncio.gather() Basics

```python
import asyncio
import random

async def fetch(name, delay):
    """Simulate fetch with delay"""
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"{name}_data"

async def main():
    # Basic gather - waits for all, returns in order
    print("=== Basic gather ===")
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("A", 0.3),
        fetch("B", 0.1),  # Finishes first
        fetch("C", 0.2),
    )
    print(f"Results (ordered): {results}")

    # Gather with tasks
    print("\n=== Gather with tasks ===")
    tasks = [
        asyncio.create_task(fetch(f"Task-{i}", random.uniform(0.1, 0.5)))
        for i in range(5)
    ]
    results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks)
    print(f"Results: {results}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 2: gather() with Exception Handling

```python
import asyncio

async def might_fail(name, should_fail):
    """Task that might raise an exception"""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    if should_fail:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} failed!")
    return f"{name}_success"

async def main():
    # Default: first exception raises
    print("=== Without return_exceptions ===")
    try:
        results = await asyncio.gather(
            might_fail("A", False),
            might_fail("B", True),   # Will fail
            might_fail("C", False),
        )
    except ValueError as e:
        print(f"Caught exception: {e}")

    # With return_exceptions: exceptions become results
    print("\n=== With return_exceptions=True ===")
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        might_fail("A", False),
        might_fail("B", True),
        might_fail("C", False),
        return_exceptions=True
    )

    for i, result in enumerate(results):
        if isinstance(result, Exception):
            print(f"Result {i}: EXCEPTION - {result}")
        else:
            print(f"Result {i}: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

#### Example 3: asyncio.wait() with Different Modes

```python
import asyncio
import random

async def variable_task(name):
    """Task with variable duration"""
    duration = random.uniform(0.5, 2.0)
    await asyncio.sleep(duration)
    return f"{name} done in {duration:.2f}s"

async def main():
    tasks = {asyncio.create_task(variable_task(f"Task-{i}")) for i in range(5)}

    # Wait for FIRST_COMPLETED
    print("=== FIRST_COMPLETED ===")
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, return_when=asyncio.FIRST_COMPLETED)

    print(f"First completed: {len(done)} tasks")
    for task in done:
        print(f"  Result: {task.result()}")
    print(f"Still pending: {len(pending)} tasks")

    # Wait for remaining
    print("\n=== Waiting for rest ===")
    done2, pending2 = await asyncio.wait(pending)
    for task in done2:
        print(f"  Result: {task.result()}")

async def wait_with_timeout():
    """Wait with timeout"""
    tasks = {asyncio.create_task(variable_task(f"Task-{i}")) for i in range(5)}

    # Wait max 1 second
    done, pending = await asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=1.0)

    print(f"\nAfter 1s timeout:")
    print(f"  Completed: {len(done)}")
    print(f"  Still pending: {len(pending)}")

    # Cancel pending tasks
    for task in pending:
        task.cancel()

    # Wait for cancellations
    await asyncio.gather(*pending, return_exceptions=True)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
    asyncio.run(wait_with_timeout())
```

diagrams.title: gather vs wait vs as_completed
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  many["Several awaitables"] --> g["gather(*aws)"]
  many --> w["wait(tasks, return_when=...)"]
  many --> ac["as_completed(aws)"]
  g --> g1["one list of results in argument order; first error propagates unless return_exceptions=True"]
  w --> w1["returns (done, pending) sets; FIRST_COMPLETED, FIRST_EXCEPTION or ALL_COMPLETED"]
  ac --> a1["iterate results in completion order — fastest first"]
diagrams.explain: Use **gather** when you want all results in order; **wait** when you need control over what happens to the pending tasks (cancel the rest, add a timeout); **as_completed** when you want to process each result as soon as it is ready. With gather, an exception does not cancel the other tasks — they keep running unless you cancel them.

sections.title: 8.5 asyncio.sleep() and Timing
sections.body:
### Code Examples

#### Example 1: Understanding asyncio.sleep()

```python
import asyncio
import time

async def demo_sleep():
    """Demonstrate asyncio.sleep()"""

    # asyncio.sleep(0) yields control to event loop
    print("About to yield...")
    await asyncio.sleep(0)  # Gives other tasks a chance to run
    print("Back!")

    # Timed sleep
    start = time.time()
    await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
    elapsed = time.time() - start
    print(f"Slept for {elapsed:.3f} seconds")

async def compare_sleep():
    """Compare time.sleep vs asyncio.sleep"""

    # time.sleep() BLOCKS the entire event loop! (Bad!)
    print("\n=== time.sleep (BLOCKING) ===")
    async def bad_task():
        print("Starting bad task...")
        time.sleep(1)  # BLOCKS everything!
        print("Bad task done")

    async def good_task(n):
        print(f"Good task {n} running")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
        print(f"Good task {n} done")

    start = time.time()
    await asyncio.gather(
        bad_task(),
        good_task(1),
        good_task(2),
    )
    print(f"Total time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Note: ~2s because time.sleep blocked everything

    # asyncio.sleep() is cooperative
    print("\n=== asyncio.sleep (COOPERATIVE) ===")
    async def nice_task():
        print("Starting nice task...")
        await asyncio.sleep(1)  # Yields to others
        print("Nice task done")

    start = time.time()
    await asyncio.gather(
        nice_task(),
        good_task(1),
        good_task(2),
    )
    print(f"Total time: {time.time() - start:.2f}s")
    # Note: ~1s because all ran concurrently

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(demo_sleep())
    asyncio.run(compare_sleep())
```

#### Example 2: Timeout with asyncio.wait_for()

```python
import asyncio

async def slow_operation():
    """Operation that takes too long"""
    await asyncio.sleep(10)
    return "finally done"

async def main():
    # With timeout
    print("=== wait_for with timeout ===")
    try:
        result = await asyncio.wait_for(slow_operation(), timeout=2.0)
        print(f"Result: {result}")
    except asyncio.TimeoutError:
        print("Operation timed out!")

    # Practical pattern: operation with timeout
    async def fetch_with_timeout(url, timeout=5.0):
        """Fetch with timeout"""
        try:
            result = await asyncio.wait_for(
                slow_operation(),  # Replace with actual fetch
                timeout=timeout
            )
            return result
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return None

    result = await fetch_with_timeout("http://example.com", timeout=1.0)
    print(f"Fetch result: {result}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())
```

diagrams.title: time.sleep blocks the loop, asyncio.sleep yields
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
  participant A as Task A
  participant L as Event loop
  participant B as Task B
  A->>L: await asyncio.sleep(1)
  L->>B: run Task B meanwhile
  B->>L: await something
  L->>A: resume A after 1 s
  Note over A,B: time.sleep(1) instead would freeze L — B cannot run for that second
diagrams.explain: `asyncio.sleep` suspends only the current task and lets the loop run others; `time.sleep` blocks the whole thread, so every task stalls. `await asyncio.sleep(0)` is a cheap way to yield control inside a long loop.

sections.title: 8.6 Running Async Code
sections.body:
### Different Ways to Run

```python
import asyncio

async def my_coroutine():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
    return "Hello"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Method 1: asyncio.run() - Recommended for scripts
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

if __name__ == "__main__":
    result = asyncio.run(my_coroutine())
    print(f"Result: {result}")

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Method 2: Get event loop manually (older style)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# loop = asyncio.get_event_loop()
# result = loop.run_until_complete(my_coroutine())
# loop.close()

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Method 3: Inside Jupyter notebooks
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# In Jupyter, you can use await directly:
# result = await my_coroutine()

# Or use nest_asyncio for nested event loops:
# import nest_asyncio
# nest_asyncio.apply()
# result = asyncio.run(my_coroutine())

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Method 4: asyncio.Runner (Python 3.11+)
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# with asyncio.Runner() as runner:
#     result1 = runner.run(my_coroutine())
#     result2 = runner.run(my_coroutine())  # Reuse same loop
```

diagrams.title: What asyncio.run(main()) does
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  r["asyncio.run(main())"] --> n["create a new event loop"] --> m["run main() to completion"] --> c["cancel leftover tasks"] --> s["shut down async generators and the default executor"] --> x["close the loop"]
diagrams.explain: `asyncio.run` is the single entry point for a program: it owns the loop's whole lifetime. Call it once, at the top level; calling it from inside a running loop raises `RuntimeError`. In Jupyter, which already runs a loop, use top-level `await` instead.

sections.title: Pitfalls & Gotchas
sections.body:
### Common Mistakes

```python
import asyncio

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# MISTAKE 1: Calling coroutine without await
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def my_coro():
    return "result"

async def wrong():
    result = my_coro()  # ❌ This returns a coroutine object!
    print(result)  # <coroutine object my_coro at 0x...>

async def right():
    result = await my_coro()  # ✅ Actually runs the coroutine
    print(result)  # "result"

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# MISTAKE 2: Using time.sleep instead of asyncio.sleep
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def blocking_bad():
    import time
    time.sleep(1)  # ❌ Blocks the entire event loop!

async def non_blocking_good():
    await asyncio.sleep(1)  # ✅ Allows other tasks to run

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# MISTAKE 3: Forgetting to await tasks
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

async def forgotten():
    task = asyncio.create_task(my_coro())
    # ❌ Function ends, task may never complete!

async def remembered():
    task = asyncio.create_task(my_coro())
    await task  # ✅ Wait for task to complete

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# MISTAKE 4: Creating tasks outside async context
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

# task = asyncio.create_task(my_coro())  # ❌ No event loop running!

async def correct():
    task = asyncio.create_task(my_coro())  # ✅ Inside async function
```

sections.title: Performance Notes
sections.body:
| Aspect      | Note                                      |
| ----------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Overhead    | Very low (~1μs per await)                 |
| Scalability | Can handle 10,000+ concurrent connections |
| Best for    | I/O-bound operations                      |
| Not for     | CPU-bound operations (blocks event loop)  |
